newsitem.title: USA: US bond market still unsure of budget pact effect.
newsitem.headline: US bond market still unsure of budget pact effect.

text.p: Although the U.S. Treasury market got what it wanted in a federal budget agreement, players remained split on Wednesday as to whether the long-awaited pact would be positive or negative for the market in the long term.

The details of last Friday's deal remain vague at best, players noted, with talks continuing on capital gains tax cuts five days after President Bill Clinton and Congressional Republican leaders hammered out an accord.
"They have an agreement to have an agreement," said one head government bond trader at a primary dealership. "It's like they are engaged.

"We don't know the details but it is an easy deal to get done," he said, noting that the budget deficit has fallen to about $70 billion from more than twice that two years ago. "There are a lot of elements that should be in (the market's favor). Net net, it's positive for the market."
Yet, players saw bumps on the road ahead before Congress and Clinton would collectively agree to a deal to balance the budget by 2002, while enacting tax and entitlement cuts.

Even though the budget deal announcement was a bullish influence for bonds, analysts do not necessarily see that sentiment continuing. It is not yet clear what the $135 billion in tax cuts over the next five years will emcompass, or whether they will be front or back-loaded.

"A budget deal was psychologically important for the market," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. "It's more symbolic than meaningful ... They could have done more."
Laughlin and others argued that the budget deal does not go far enough in cutting Medicare and Medicaid spending.

"What's there to like? It does little to address the structural problems in the deficit," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "I look at it as a negative, not a positive (for the market). We declared victory, but there are problems out there, and we won't address them again until we get a crisis."
Liro, though, said that he was not surprised at the market's response, since it also rallied on budget pacts in 1990 and 1993 and on a potential but failed budget try in late 1995.
"This (budget) is not a reason to rally," he said. "It needs some entitlement reform and some measure to get Social Security under control."
But market participants doubt anything like that will happen.

"It is going to be difficult (for Congress) not to pass the budget in the form which was agreed to," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc. "Extreme conservatives will not be happy and liberal Democrats will not be happy.
"But it is something the middle of the road of both parties will adopt and that's why it will pass," he added.

Still, Lieberman does not see a budget pact as a big deal for the economy and near-term Federal Reserve policy. "We don't know if it is net stimulative or net restrictive to the economy. But it is not likely to be highly stimulative or restrictive in 1998," he said.
Earlier on Wednesday, San Francisco Fed research director Jack Beebe told Reuters that the balanced budget agreement reached last week is unlikely to change the way the Fed will conduct policy.
"I don't think this (accord) is enough of a change in the direction of fiscal policy to matter a great deal to the way monetary policy has to be managed over the next several years," Beebe said.
As such, players said the market will likely settle in and put the budget issue aside for now to concentrate on upcoming economic news and supply.
"There are a lot of reasons for the market to rally," said Liro, "and the budget is the least of them."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
